CONSTITUTION OF HOPEBRIDGE SINGAPORE
(Adopted 1 January 2022; amended 15 March 2023)

NAME
The name of the society shall be HOPEBRIDGE SINGAPORE, hereinafter referred to as "the Society".

PLACE OF BUSINESS
The Society shall carry on its activities in Singapore. The registered address of the Society shall be 10 Anson Road, #25-08 International Plaza, Singapore 079903, or such other address as the Management Committee may from time to time determine.

OBJECTS
The objects of the Society are as set out in the Certificate of Registration.

MEMBERSHIP
Ordinary membership shall be open to persons aged 18 years and above who support the objects of the Society. The Management Committee shall have the power to approve or reject applications for membership.

MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE
The affairs of the Society shall be managed by a Management Committee comprising not less than five and not more than twelve members, elected at the Annual General Meeting.

GRANTS COMMITTEE
1. There shall be a Grants Committee, appointed by the Management Committee, comprising not less than three members.
2. The Grants Committee shall be responsible for the governance of the Society's grant-making functions, including the Community Impact Fund.
3. The Grants Committee shall consider applications for funding, make recommendations to the Management Committee, and oversee the disbursement of approved grants.
4. The Grants Committee shall report to the Management Committee at each regular meeting.

COMMUNITY IMPACT FUND
The Community Impact Fund shall be a programme of the Society, established to provide financial support to community-based projects that align with the objects of the Society.

FINANCIAL YEAR
The financial year of the Society shall end on 31 December each year.

AMENDMENTS
This Constitution may be amended by a resolution passed by not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting at a General Meeting.

This is to certify that the following amendments to the Constitution of HopeBridge Singapore were duly passed by a resolution of the members at an Extraordinary General Meeting held on 12 November 2022, and subsequently approved by the Registry of Societies on 30 January 2023.

Amendment 1: Establishment of the Grants Committee
The Constitution is amended by inserting a new clause, numbered 12A, after the existing Clause 12 (Powers of the Management Committee). The new clause reads as follows:

12A. Grants Committee
(a) There shall be established a Grants Committee of the Society, which shall have the authority to consider, approve, and oversee all grant-making activities of the Society.
(b) The Grants Committee shall comprise no fewer than three (3) and no more than seven (7) members, all of whom shall be appointed by the Management Committee.
(c) The Honorary Treasurer shall serve as an ex-officio member of the Grants Committee.
(d) The Grants Committee shall meet at least once per calendar quarter, and shall report on its activities to the Management Committee at each ordinary meeting of the Management Committee.
(e) No grant shall be disbursed without the written approval of the Grants Committee, recorded in the minutes of a duly convened meeting.

Amendment 2: Approval of Internal Policies
The Constitution is amended by inserting a new clause, numbered 12B, after the new Clause 12A. The new clause reads as follows:

12B. Internal Policies
(a) The Management Committee shall have the power to adopt, amend, or revoke internal policies of the Society, including but not limited to policies relating to financial controls, procurement, data protection, volunteer management, and safeguarding.
(b) All internal policies shall be tabled for information at the next Annual General Meeting following their adoption.
(c) A copy of all current internal policies shall be maintained by the Honorary Secretary and made available to members upon written request.

Amendment 3: Registered Office
The Constitution is amended by deleting the words "the registered office of the Society shall be at such place in Singapore as the Management Committee may from time to time determine" and substituting the following: "the registered office of the Society shall be at 10 Anson Road, #25-08 International Plaza, Singapore 079903, or at such other place in Singapore as the Management Committee may from time to time determine with the prior approval of the Registry of Societies."

**3.1 Sunrise Youth Centre (SYC)**

**Proposal Reference:** SYC-2023-014

**Programme Title:** "Taking Flight" – Outreach and Mentoring Programme for At-Risk Youth

**Requested Amount:** SGD 50,000

**Proposed Duration:** 12 months (1 July 2023 – 30 June 2024)

**Summary of Proposal:** SYC seeks funding to expand its street outreach and one-on-one mentoring programme for youth aged 13–18 in the Tampines and Bedok areas. The programme aims to engage 120 at-risk youth through regular outreach sessions, structured mentoring, and referral pathways to education, training, and employment support. The proposal includes staffing costs for two outreach workers, training materials, and a small activities budget.

**Presentation and Discussion:**
The SYC Programme Director, Ms. Rachel Lim, presented the proposal. She highlighted that SYC has been operating for 12 years and has an established track record in youth outreach. The organisation reported that referral rates from schools and social services have increased by 30% over the past two years, and demand for mentoring slots currently exceeds capacity.

Committee members discussed the following points:
- The proposal aligns with the Foundation's strategic priority on youth resilience and employability.
- The budget was considered reasonable, with clearly itemised costs. No significant concerns were raised regarding the staffing cost breakdown.
- Dr. Wei Ming queried the monitoring and evaluation framework. Ms. Lim confirmed that SYC will report on output indicators (number of youth engaged, number of mentoring sessions completed) and outcome indicators (school re-engagement, referral completion rates) on a quarterly basis.
- Priya Raman noted the strong collaboration with local schools and the police's neighbourhood policing centres, which was viewed positively.

**Decision:**
*Motion:* That the Grants Committee approves the grant amount of SGD 50,000 to Sunrise Youth Centre for the "Taking Flight" programme, subject to the standard terms and conditions of the Foundation's grant agreement.

Existing Gaps
While several mental health services operate in the region, most are clinic-based, require formal referrals, or carry fee structures that deter lower-income residents. Community gardening programmes exist in other parts of Singapore but are primarily recreational, lacking structured therapeutic components or trained facilitation. There is currently no dedicated nature-based mental wellness programme in the Queenstown area that combines horticultural therapy with peer support.

Why Nature-Based Intervention?
Evidence from the National University of Singapore's Department of Psychology (2021) suggests that structured engagement with green spaces reduces cortisol levels, improves mood, and enhances social connectedness. The therapeutic benefits of horticulture are well-documented in international literature, and Singapore's tropical climate permits year-round gardening activities. Project Bloom adapts proven models from the UK's Thrive programme and Australia's Community Gardens Australia framework, localising them to Singapore's public housing context.

SECTION D: PROJECT OBJECTIVES AND OUTCOMES

Objective 1: Establish three accessible community garden nodes
Outcome 1.1: Three garden sites operational by Month 6
Outcome 1.2: Each garden node has a minimum of 40 planting beds accessible to wheelchair users
Outcome 1.3: Gardens are open to the public at least 6 days per week

Objective 2: Train resident volunteer facilitators
Outcome 2.1: 30 volunteers complete a 40-hour facilitator training programme
Outcome 2.2: At least 25 volunteers remain active beyond Month 12
Outcome 2.3: Volunteers achieve competency in horticultural basics, group facilitation, and mental health first aid

Objective 3: Deliver the "Grow & Ground" therapeutic programme
Outcome 3.1: 1,200 participants complete at least 8 of 12 programme sessions
Outcome 3.2: Participants report a 30% reduction in self-assessed stress levels (measured via PSS-10 scale)
Outcome 3.3: 80% of participants report improved social connectedness (measured via UCLA Loneliness Scale)

Objective 4: Foster programme sustainability
Outcome 4.1: A volunteer-led steering committee established by Month 12
Outcome 4.2: 70% of programme costs covered by community fundraising and in-kind contributions by Month 18
Outcome 4.3: Programme manual and training toolkit published and freely available online

SECTION E: PROJECT ACTIVITIES AND METHODOLOGY

Phase 1: Site Preparation and Community Engagement (Months 1–6)

Activity 1.1: Site identification and partnership agreements
GCC will work with the Housing & Development Board (HDB) and National Parks Board (NParks) to secure permission for garden sites. Three locations have been identified as preliminary candidates: Commonwealth Crescent Community Garden (existing), Margaret Drive Open Space (underutilised), and a rooftop garden at Block 47 Holland Drive (to be confirmed). Formal agreements will be signed by Month 3.

Activity 1.2: Community consultation sessions
Six town hall-style consultation sessions will be conducted (two per precinct) to gather resident input on garden design, programme scheduling, and cultural sensitivities. Feedback will inform the final garden layout and programme calendar.

Activity 1.3: Garden infrastructure development
Each site will receive raised planting beds (at accessible heights), a tool storage shed, a rainwater harvesting system, and shaded seating areas. NParks will provide technical guidance on soil quality and native plant selection. A landscape architect will be engaged on a consultancy basis.

Phase 2: Volunteer Recruitment and Training (Months 4–8)

Activity 2.1: Volunteer recruitment drive
Recruitment will target residents aged 18–70, with a focus on retirees, stay-at-home parents, and young professionals seeking meaningful community engagement. Recruitment channels include grassroots organisation newsletters, social media, and referrals from existing community partners.

**2. SITE OVERVIEW & FACILITY INSPECTION**

LCC operates from a two-storey former school building at 12 Lakeside Drive, Singapore 648201. The centre shares the compound with a community garden and a small multi-purpose court. The building is in good repair overall. The main hall, four programme rooms, and the administrative office were all accessible and in use during the visit.

Facility observations:

- Main hall (capacity approx. 120): Used for weekly seniors' exercise classes and weekend family activities. Flooring appeared recently cleaned; chairs and tables were stacked neatly at the side.
- Programme rooms (Rooms 1–4): Room 2 was set up for an afternoon youth workshop (materials on tables, projector tested and working). Rooms 1, 3, and 4 were being used for small group sessions. No overcrowding observed.
- Storage room: Locked and organised. Ms. Wong confirmed that all programme materials are logged in/out using the centre's register.
- Toilets and pantry: Clean; no obvious maintenance or safety issues. The pantry has a new water dispenser (installed June 2023) and a working refrigerator.
- Community garden: Well-maintained, with several volunteers present during the visit. The garden is used for intergenerational activities and produce donation to nearby rental blocks.

No significant facility-related concerns identified.

---

**3. PROGRAMME OBSERVATIONS**

LCC is currently running three main programmes under the grant: (a) Seniors' Wellness & Befriending, (b) Youth Mentorship & Skills, and (c) Family Food Support (includes the community garden component).

**3.1 Seniors' Wellness & Befriending**

Observed the 09:30–10:30 exercise class. Attendance was 24 seniors (target for the session was 25). The instructor, a contracted fitness trainer, was present and led the session appropriately. Participants appeared engaged. Ms. Wong noted that the programme has a waiting list of 12 seniors, and the centre is exploring adding a second weekly session. Volunteer befrienders (6 active) conduct home visits on weekday afternoons; visit logs were reviewed and appeared up to date.

**3.2 Youth Mentorship & Skills**

The programme is in its second cycle, with 18 youths enrolled (ages 13–17). Mr. Tan reported that the current cycle focuses on digital literacy and basic financial management. The youth workshop observed (11:00–12:30) was on budgeting and using mobile banking apps; the facilitator was from a partner organisation. Attendance for the session was 14 of 18; Mr. Tan explained that two youths had notified the centre in advance of other commitments, and two were absent without notice. The centre follows up on unexcused absences within two working days.

Mentor-youth matching records were reviewed. All 18 youths have a designated mentor. Mentor background checks and training records are on file and current. Two mentor-youth matches were noted as inactive since July 2023 (mentor had to step down due to work commitments); Mr. Tan confirmed that replacements have been identified and are in the onboarding process.

**3.3 Family Food Support & Community Garden**

The food support programme operates a weekly distribution every Saturday morning. The last distribution was on 5 August 2023; 52 families collected food parcels (average for recent weeks is 50–55 families). The centre also runs a referral system with nearby social service offices.

The community garden is used to grow vegetables (kangkong, bayam, chye sim, and some herbs). Produce harvested is added to the food parcels. Volunteer gardeners maintain a planting and harvest schedule, which was reviewed and appears realistic. During the visit, two volunteers were harvesting vegetables for the upcoming distribution.

**3. GRANT PROPOSALS FOR CONSIDERATION**

The Committee considered three grant proposals under the Q2 2023 disbursement cycle. Proposals were circulated to members seven days in advance. Each applicant organisation was invited to give a brief presentation during the meeting.

**3.1 Sunrise Youth Centre (SYC)**

**Proposal Reference:** SYC-2023-014

**Programme Title:** "Taking Flight" – Outreach and Mentoring Programme for At-Risk Youth

**Requested Amount:** SGD 50,000

**Proposed Duration:** 12 months (1 July 2023 – 30 June 2024)

**Summary of Proposal:** SYC seeks funding to expand its street outreach and one-on-one mentoring programme for youth aged 13–18 in the Tampines and Bedok areas. The programme aims to engage 120 at-risk youth through regular outreach sessions, structured mentoring, and referral pathways to education, training, and employment support. The proposal includes staffing costs for two outreach workers, training materials, and a small activities budget.

**Presentation and Discussion:**
The SYC Programme Director, Ms. Rachel Lim, presented the proposal. She highlighted that SYC has been operating for 12 years and has an established track record in youth outreach. The organisation reported that referral rates from schools and social services have increased by 30% over the past two years, and demand for mentoring slots currently exceeds capacity.

Committee members discussed the following points:
- The proposal aligns with the Foundation's strategic priority on youth resilience and employability.
- The budget was considered reasonable, with clearly itemised costs. No significant concerns were raised regarding the staffing cost breakdown.
- Dr. Wei Ming queried the monitoring and evaluation framework. Ms. Lim confirmed that SYC will report on output indicators (number of youth engaged, number of mentoring sessions completed) and outcome indicators (school re-engagement, referral completion rates) on a quarterly basis.
- Priya Raman noted the strong collaboration with local schools and the police's neighbourhood policing centres, which was viewed positively.

**Decision:**
*Motion:* That the Grants Committee approves the grant amount of SGD 50,000 to Sunrise Youth Centre for the "Taking Flight" programme, subject to the standard terms and conditions of the Foundation's grant agreement.

The Grants Committee minutes record that Sunrise Youth Centre's grant amount approved was 50000 SGD. Record status: current.

*Moved by:* Dr. Wei Ming
*Seconded by:* Faridah Ismail

*Vote:* 7 in favour, 0 against, 0 abstentions. Motion carried unanimously.

**Rationale:** The proposal was assessed as high quality and well-aligned with the Foundation's strategic objectives. The requested amount of SGD 50,000 is within the budget envelope for this disbursement cycle. The Grants Committee minutes record that Sunrise Youth Centre's grant amount approved was 50000 SGD, which remains the current approved allocation for this programme. The Committee noted the organisation's strong track record and the clear articulation of intended outcomes.

**Conditions:**
- The grant agreement must be signed by 15 June 2023.
- First disbursement of SGD 25,000 will be released upon receipt of the signed agreement. The remaining SGD 25,000 will be released upon receipt of the first quarterly progress report, due by 15 October 2023.
- Quarterly progress reports and financial statements are to be submitted in accordance with the Foundation's reporting schedule.

---

**3.2 GreenCare Collective**

**Proposal Reference:** GCC-2023-007

**Programme Title:** Community Food Waste Reduction and Composting Initiative

**Requested Amount:** SGD 32,000

**Proposed Duration:** 18 months (1 August 2023 – 31 January 2025)

**Summary of Proposal:** GreenCare Collective proposes to establish community composting hubs at three locations in the Yishun area, working with hawker centres and residents to divert food waste from incineration. The programme includes public education workshops, distribution of compost bins, and a partnership with the National Environment Agency.

---

**1. Minutes of Previous Meeting**

The minutes of the Grants Committee meeting held on 28 June 2023 were circulated in advance. No amendments were proposed. The minutes were confirmed as a true record.

---

**2. Project Updates and Budget Reviews**

**2.1 Sunrise Youth Centre – "Taking Flight" Programme**

The Committee noted the progress update for the "Taking Flight" programme, for which a grant of SGD 50,000 was approved at the June meeting. The grant agreement was signed on 10 June 2023, ahead of the 15 June deadline. The first disbursement of SGD 25,000 was released on 16 June 2023.

The first quarterly progress report was received on 2 October 2023, ahead of the 15 October due date. The report indicates that the programme has commenced as planned, with 120 youth enrolled across three cohorts. The Committee noted that the second disbursement of SGD 25,000 will be released upon review of the progress report by the programme team. No concerns were raised.

**2.2 GreenCare Collective – Community Food Waste Reduction and Composting Initiative**

The Committee received a project update for GreenCare Collective (Proposal Reference: GCC-2023-007). The grant agreement GA-2023-018 was signed on 15 August 2023. The first disbursement was released on 1 September 2023.

The update indicates that site assessments for the three proposed composting hubs in the Yishun area have been completed. Two hawker centres have confirmed their participation, and the third is pending final approval from the town council. The partnership discussions with the National Environment Agency are ongoing. The Committee noted that the programme is on track, with the first public education workshop scheduled for 18 November 2023.

The Committee requested that the next update include a breakdown of volunteer recruitment figures, as this was not provided in the current update.

**2.3 Lakeside Community Centre – Budget Review**

The Committee reviewed the budget utilisation for Lakeside Community Centre's existing grant. The centre has utilised approximately 68% of its approved grant to date. The Committee noted that the remaining funds are earmarked for the upcoming Deepavali community celebration and the year-end youth programme. No issues were raised regarding the budget utilisation.

---

**3. New Grant Proposals – Discussion and Decisions**

**3.1 Lakeside Community Centre – "Digital Literacy for Seniors" Programme**

**Proposal Reference:** LCC-2023-014

**Programme Title:** Digital Literacy for Seniors: Bridging the Digital Divide

**Requested Amount:** SGD 28,000

**Proposed Duration:** 12 months (1 January 2024 – 31 December 2024)

**Summary of Proposal:** Lakeside Community Centre proposes to conduct weekly digital literacy workshops for seniors aged 60 and above. The programme will cover basic smartphone usage, online safety, and access to government digital services. The centre will recruit volunteer trainers and partner with the local library for venue support.

**Discussion:** The Committee discussed the proposal's alignment with the Foundation's strategic objective of promoting digital inclusion. Members noted the organisation's strong track record in community outreach. The Committee discussed the proposed budget, particularly the allocation for equipment purchases. It was noted that the centre has existing computers that could be utilised, potentially reducing the equipment cost.

**Decision:** The proposal was approved in principle. The Committee requested that the organisation revise the budget to reflect the use of existing equipment and resubmit the proposal for final approval. The revised proposal is to be submitted by 31 October 2023.

documents.title: Grant Proposal: GreenCare Collective
documents.content:
Existing Gaps
While several mental health services operate in the region, most are clinic-based, require formal referrals, or carry fee structures that deter lower-income residents. Community gardening programmes exist in other parts of Singapore but are primarily recreational, lacking structured therapeutic components or trained facilitation. There is currently no dedicated nature-based mental wellness programme in the Queenstown area that combines horticultural therapy with peer support.

Why Nature-Based Intervention?
Evidence from the National University of Singapore's Department of Psychology (2021) suggests that structured engagement with green spaces reduces cortisol levels, improves mood, and enhances social connectedness. The therapeutic benefits of horticulture are well-documented in international literature, and Singapore's tropical climate permits year-round gardening activities. Project Bloom adapts proven models from the UK's Thrive programme and Australia's Community Gardens Australia framework, localising them to Singapore's public housing context.

SECTION D: PROJECT OBJECTIVES AND OUTCOMES

Objective 1: Establish three accessible community garden nodes
Outcome 1.1: Three garden sites operational by Month 6
Outcome 1.2: Each garden node has a minimum of 40 planting beds accessible to wheelchair users
Outcome 1.3: Gardens are open to the public at least 6 days per week

Objective 2: Train resident volunteer facilitators
Outcome 2.1: 30 volunteers complete a 40-hour facilitator training programme
Outcome 2.2: At least 25 volunteers remain active beyond Month 12
Outcome 2.3: Volunteers achieve competency in horticultural basics, group facilitation, and mental health first aid

Objective 3: Deliver the "Grow & Ground" therapeutic programme
Outcome 3.1: 1,200 participants complete at least 8 of 12 programme sessions
Outcome 3.2: Participants report a 30% reduction in self-assessed stress levels (measured via PSS-10 scale)
Outcome 3.3: 80% of participants report improved social connectedness (measured via UCLA Loneliness Scale)

Objective 4: Foster programme sustainability
Outcome 4.1: A volunteer-led steering committee established by Month 12
Outcome 4.2: 70% of programme costs covered by community fundraising and in-kind contributions by Month 18
Outcome 4.3: Programme manual and training toolkit published and freely available online

GreenCare Collective proposal_submitted_on 2023-04-01 date. Record status: historical.

SECTION E: PROJECT ACTIVITIES AND METHODOLOGY

Phase 1: Site Preparation and Community Engagement (Months 1–6)

Activity 1.1: Site identification and partnership agreements
GCC will work with the Housing & Development Board (HDB) and National Parks Board (NParks) to secure permission for garden sites. Three locations have been identified as preliminary candidates: Commonwealth Crescent Community Garden (existing), Margaret Drive Open Space (underutilised), and a rooftop garden at Block 47 Holland Drive (to be confirmed). Formal agreements will be signed by Month 3.

Activity 1.2: Community consultation sessions
Six town hall-style consultation sessions will be conducted (two per precinct) to gather resident input on garden design, programme scheduling, and cultural sensitivities. Feedback will inform the final garden layout and programme calendar.

Activity 1.3: Garden infrastructure development
Each site will receive raised planting beds (at accessible heights), a tool storage shed, a rainwater harvesting system, and shaded seating areas. NParks will provide technical guidance on soil quality and native plant selection. A landscape architect will be engaged on a consultancy basis.

Phase 2: Volunteer Recruitment and Training (Months 4–8)

Activity 2.1: Volunteer recruitment drive
Recruitment will target residents aged 18–70, with a focus on retirees, stay-at-home parents, and young professionals seeking meaningful community engagement. Recruitment channels include grassroots organisation newsletters, social media, and referrals from existing community partners.

documents.title: Field Monitor Report: Lakeside Community Centre
documents.content:
---

**2. SITE OVERVIEW & FACILITY INSPECTION**

LCC operates from a two-storey former school building at 12 Lakeside Drive, Singapore 648201. The centre shares the compound with a community garden and a small multi-purpose court. The building is in good repair overall. The main hall, four programme rooms, and the administrative office were all accessible and in use during the visit.

Facility observations:

- Main hall (capacity approx. 120): Used for weekly seniors' exercise classes and weekend family activities. Flooring appeared recently cleaned; chairs and tables were stacked neatly at the side.
- Programme rooms (Rooms 1–4): Room 2 was set up for an afternoon youth workshop (materials on tables, projector tested and working). Rooms 1, 3, and 4 were being used for small group sessions. No overcrowding observed.
- Storage room: Locked and organised. Ms. Wong confirmed that all programme materials are logged in/out using the centre's register.
- Toilets and pantry: Clean; no obvious maintenance or safety issues. The pantry has a new water dispenser (installed June 2023) and a working refrigerator.
- Community garden: Well-maintained, with several volunteers present during the visit. The garden is used for intergenerational activities and produce donation to nearby rental blocks.

No significant facility-related concerns identified.

---

**3. PROGRAMME OBSERVATIONS**

LCC is currently running three main programmes under the grant: (a) Seniors' Wellness & Befriending, (b) Youth Mentorship & Skills, and (c) Family Food Support (includes the community garden component).

**3.1 Seniors' Wellness & Befriending**

Observed the 09:30–10:30 exercise class. Attendance was 24 seniors (target for the session was 25). The instructor, a contracted fitness trainer, was present and led the session appropriately. Participants appeared engaged. Ms. Wong noted that the programme has a waiting list of 12 seniors, and the centre is exploring adding a second weekly session. Volunteer befrienders (6 active) conduct home visits on weekday afternoons; visit logs were reviewed and appeared up to date.

**3.2 Youth Mentorship & Skills**

Lakeside Community Centre monitoring_visit_date 2023-08-10 date. Record status: historical.

The programme is in its second cycle, with 18 youths enrolled (ages 13–17). Mr. Tan reported that the current cycle focuses on digital literacy and basic financial management. The youth workshop observed (11:00–12:30) was on budgeting and using mobile banking apps; the facilitator was from a partner organisation. Attendance for the session was 14 of 18; Mr. Tan explained that two youths had notified the centre in advance of other commitments, and two were absent without notice. The centre follows up on unexcused absences within two working days.

Mentor-youth matching records were reviewed. All 18 youths have a designated mentor. Mentor background checks and training records are on file and current. Two mentor-youth matches were noted as inactive since July 2023 (mentor had to step down due to work commitments); Mr. Tan confirmed that replacements have been identified and are in the onboarding process.

**3.3 Family Food Support & Community Garden**

The food support programme operates a weekly distribution every Saturday morning. The last distribution was on 5 August 2023; 52 families collected food parcels (average for recent weeks is 50–55 families). The centre also runs a referral system with nearby social service offices.

The community garden is used to grow vegetables (kangkong, bayam, chye sim, and some herbs). Produce harvested is added to the food parcels. Volunteer gardeners maintain a planting and harvest schedule, which was reviewed and appears realistic. During the visit, two volunteers were harvesting vegetables for the upcoming distribution.

---

**Overall Compliance Rating: Compliant**

No major or minor compliance issues were identified during this visit.
